messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military, Self-Consciousness: Being seen, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible, People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi Singh is a 41-year-old park ranger who came to treatment after months of insisting to his girlfriend that he was “fine” and then, one afternoon at work, dropping to the ground when a coworker stepped suddenly out from behind a maintenance shed. The reaction embarrassed him more than it frightened him. He was seen by two seasonal staff members, and afterward he could not shake the feeling that they had witnessed something shameful and irreversible about him. By the time he sought help, what weighed on him most was not only how often he felt on edge, but the conviction that what happened to him had marked him in a way other people could not understand.

The traumatic event occurred while he was traveling in a remote area several years earlier. He was taken and held against his will by armed men in uniform. What remained with him was not a single flowing narrative so much as a set of hard, fixed images: the first sight of a sleeve patch and rifle sling as he realized he was not free to leave; the close view of a door shutting; a face leaning near his while he was being watched; the angle of a boot beside him as he tried not to move; the sensation of pain in his body while he was confined and powerless. When he describes the experience now, it often comes in these still frames. At other times he can recount facts about where he was held and for how long in a flat, detached way, as if he is describing something that happened to someone else. He notices that both states are unsettling in different ways: either the memory strikes him as if it is happening in the present, or he feels nothing and is left disturbed by his own numbness.

Certain cues in daily life carry an immediate charge because they resemble those moments. Visitors to the park sometimes strike up conversations about military service or current conflicts, especially at the trailhead kiosk where Ravi checks permits. He finds himself going rigid while nodding politely, his attention narrowing onto bits of uniform, insignia, or the cadence of the conversation. People in uniform are particularly difficult. State troopers, search-and-rescue teams, even certain utility workers can set him on edge before they have said a word. He becomes acutely self-conscious when he feels watched, as though being seen too closely means being exposed and trapped again. On busy days he positions himself so he has a clear line of sight and dislikes having anyone approach from the side. Unexpected movement nearby can make him jerk, step back, or raise an arm defensively before he knows what he is doing.

When the experience breaks through more fully, Ravi sometimes has the sense that the captivity is happening again. In those moments he is no longer standing in a park office or on a trail but back inside those few terrible images, and he feels pain in the same parts of his body that hurt during the ordeal. He has learned not to trust reassurance. When his girlfriend tells him he is home and safe, or when colleagues tell him there is no danger, he hears the words but cannot make himself believe them. Safety feels to him like something other people talk about more easily than they know.

Over time he has developed small, rigid routines that help him feel less exposed. He tightly controls what and when he eats, experiencing the discipline as one of the few things that is fully his to command. At work he is overly agreeable with supervisors, law enforcement partners, and even demanding visitors, going along quickly with what others want because compliance feels safer than risking conflict with anyone who has authority. The cost has been quiet but significant. Coworkers know him as dependable, but some have noticed he never pushes back, even when he is overloaded. At home, his girlfriend has become frustrated by how little he tells her and by his tendency to shut down after public incidents that leave him feeling observed.

He is also troubled by thoughts he does not like admitting: vivid fantasies of revenge against the people responsible for his captivity. He does not describe any plan or intention, but the fantasies come as a private counterweight to the humiliation he carries. He has come to believe that what happened revealed something weak in him, that another man would have found a way out or would not have ended up captive at all. Around other people he often feels fundamentally separate, as if there is an invisible boundary between him and those who have not been degraded in the same way.

What finally brought Ravi in was the accumulation of these moments at work and the fear that they were beginning to define his life. He worries most about being seen as broken, especially in uniformed settings or in front of younger staff he supervises informally in the park. At the same time, he says he wants “to stop living like every movement means something is about to happen,” and to find some way of being with the memories without either falling into them or going completely numb.
